messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 52
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: In a relationship
- Occupation: Film Director
- Trauma Type: Life-threatening accident
- Pcl5: 35

# Marcus

Marcus is a 52-year-old film director who has spent the better part of three decades constructing worlds for other people to inhabit — controlling light, sound, movement, and meaning with practiced authority. He is the kind of man who has always felt most comfortable behind the camera, where everything that enters the frame does so because he has decided it should. That sense of control is something he no longer entirely trusts.

Fourteen months ago, Marcus was driving home from a location scout in the hills outside the city when a truck drifted across the centre line and struck his car head-on. The impact was severe enough to require the fire service to cut him free. He was conscious throughout — a detail he returns to again and again. He remembers the smell of antifreeze and something burning, the strange quality of the afternoon light through a shattered windscreen, and the particular silence that followed the collision before the pain arrived. He walked away with a fractured clavicle, three broken ribs, and a laceration along his left forearm that required forty-two stitches. The truck driver was uninjured. Marcus found this fact difficult to process for reasons he cannot fully articulate.

The physical recovery took several months. What has not recovered, or has not recovered in the same way, is harder to name. In the weeks following the accident, Marcus began waking between three and four in the morning with his heart already racing, certain — for a few disorienting seconds — that the impact was happening again. He would lie in the dark beside his partner, Elena, unable to explain why he could not simply go back to sleep. He has not told her the full extent of what those nights feel like.

Driving remains a significant problem. Marcus returned to the wheel after about six weeks because his work demanded it, but he describes highway driving as something he now endures rather than performs. He sits rigidly, watches the mirrors compulsively, and finds himself rehearsing escape routes when trucks appear in adjacent lanes. On two occasions he has pulled off the motorway without being able to say exactly why, sitting in a lay-by until the tightness in his chest subsided. He has begun delegating more location scouts to his assistant director, framing it as a shift in his working style rather than an avoidance.

On set, colleagues have noticed that Marcus is less patient than he used to be. He is aware of this himself and is quietly ashamed of it. He describes a persistent low-level irritability that he cannot always explain or control, a sense of being faintly braced against something that has not yet arrived. Loud, sudden sounds — a clapper board snapping, a piece of equipment falling — produce a startle response that he finds embarrassing in a professional environment where he is expected to project calm authority. He has become more reliant on meticulous pre-production planning, he says, though he acknowledges this may be less about craft and more about managing his own anxiety.

There are stretches of days, sometimes longer, when things feel almost normal. He can lose himself in the editing suite, in the close and absorbing work of assembling footage, and for hours at a time the accident recedes. He values this. He describes editing as the one place where he still feels like himself — where the world is manageable, sequential, and responsive to his decisions.

But the accident has changed something in his relationship to his own imagination. He is currently in pre-production on a new film, a road thriller, and he has found himself unable to watch the crash sequences his second unit has been filming. He sits outside the screening room while the footage runs, telling himself he will go in shortly. He has not gone in yet. He has not told his producer.

Marcus presents as composed, articulate, and somewhat reluctant to assign weight to his own experience. He mentions, almost in passing, that he has always believed people who make films about suffering ought to be able to tolerate a certain amount of it themselves.
